This Ukrainian-born lawyer served as prosecutor of Crimea before becoming Russia's ambassador to Cape Verde and a State Duma deputy — who is she?
Consisting of right view, right speech, and six other 'right' practices, this early Buddhist teaching charts the way toward liberation from the cycle of rebirth — what is it called?
Noble Eightfold Path: Buddhist practices leading to liberation from saṃsāra.
In Christian theology, this condition inherited from Adam and Eve's expulsion from Eden was shaped significantly by Augustine of Hippo — what is it called?
Original sin: Christian doctrine about human nature.
An economist who began as a Madrid city councillor in 2004, he's led Spain's Socialist Workers' Party and, since 2022, presided over Socialist International — which prime minister is it?
Pedro Sánchez: Prime Minister of Spain since 2018. Sánchez began his political career in August 2004 as a city councillor in Madrid, before being elected to the Congress of Deputies in 2009.

Head of the Catholic Church for nearly 32 years — the longest verified reign in history — this pontiff convened a council that defined papal infallibility before declaring himself a 'prisoner' after Rome's capture in 1870 — who was he?
Pope Pius IX: Head of the Catholic Church from 1846 to 1878.
This ideology holds that humans split into groups ranked as inherently superior or inferior, based on supposedly inherited and shared traits — what is it called?
Declared independent on a man-made platform in the Adriatic in 1968, this micronation used Esperanto as its official language before being demolished by Italian authorities — what was it called?
Republic of Rose Island: 1968 micronation in the Adriatic Sea. The Italian government viewed it as a ploy by Rosa to raise money from tourists while avoiding national taxation.
Born in Tampico, Illinois, this future actor started as a sports broadcaster in Iowa in 1933 before moving to Hollywood and later serving as Screen Actors Guild president twice. Who was he?
Ronald Reagan: President of the United States from 1981 to 1989.

In 1982 this child from Manchester, Maine wrote a letter to Soviet leader Yuri Andropov — and got a personal reply inviting her to visit the USSR, making her 'America's Youngest Ambassador' — who was she?
Samantha Smith: American child peace activist (1972–1985)
Founded in 312 BC by one of Alexander the Great's generals, this Hellenistic Greek state stretched from Anatolia to Afghanistan before Pompey folded it into Rome — which state was it?
Seleucid Empire: Hellenistic state in West Asia (312–63 BC)
Nicknamed "the firebrand," this radical feminist helped found three New York organizations and in 1968 staged a symbolic "Burial of Traditional Womanhood" — who was she?

In July 1995, more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in and around a town the UN had declared a 'safe area' — an event now recognized as the first legally proven genocide in Europe since World War II. What is it called?
Srebrenica massacre: 1995 genocidal killing of Bosniak Muslim men.
In 2007 this French politician became the first woman to reach the second round of a presidential election, ultimately losing to Nicolas Sarkozy — who is she?
Known as 'the Great,' this Roman emperor was the last to rule the entire empire single-handedly and helped enshrine the Nicene Creed as orthodox doctrine — who was he?
Theodosius I: Roman emperor from 379 to 395.

Breaking out in 1990 between Moldovan government forces and pro-separatist fighters backed by Russia's 14th Army, this conflict over a breakaway region ended with a ceasefire in July 1992 that still holds — which conflict?
Transnistrian War: 1990–1992 separatist conflict in Moldova. Cojocaru, the Moldovan defeat in this war directly led to implementation of Moldovan neutrality.
Born in Jaffna, this guerrilla leader founded and led a militant organization in a decades-long campaign for an independent Tamil state in Sri Lanka — who is he?
Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine
Velupillai Prabhakaran: Leader of militant Tamil organisation in Sri Lanka (1954–2009)

Once a close ally of Sun Yat-sen and celebrated for his part in the 1911 Revolution, this Chinese politician later led a Japanese-backed puppet government in WWII and is remembered by many as a traitor — who is he?
Kenya's current president since 2022, he previously became the country's first elected deputy president after representing Eldoret North in parliament — who is he?

William Ruto: President of Kenya since 2022. William Kipchirchir Samoei Arap Ruto (born 21 December 1966) is a Kenyan politician who is the fifth and current president of Kenya since 13 September 2022.
Before serving two terms as Israel's seventh prime minister, this Polish-born politician had been a leader of the pre-state Zionist militant group Lehi, the so-called Stern Gang — who was he?
Yitzhak Shamir: Prime Minister of Israel (1983–1984; 1986–1992)

This Sanskrit term translating as 'emptiness' or 'voidness' anchors a key Mahāyāna Buddhist tenet, and in Theravāda often points to the non-self nature of the five aggregates of experience — what is it?
Śūnyatā: Philosophical concept of emptiness found in Asian religions.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these people was born first?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt (born 1868) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
William Osler (born 1849) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these came out first?
MUMPS (published 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Alessandro Volta is a physicist. Throughout his life, Volta enjoyed a certain amount of closeness with the emperor who conferred upon him numerous honours.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Samuel Conway is a chemist. Samuel Charles Conway (born June 4, 1965) is an American researcher in the pharmaceutical, biomedical and agrochemical fields of organic chemistry.
What is the atomic number of Lithium?
Lithium (from Ancient Greek: λίθος, líthos, 'stone') is a chemical element; it has symbol Li and atomic number 3.
In what year was Blaise Pascal born?
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
In what year was Friedrich Engels born?
Friedrich Engels: After Marx's death, Engels served as the editor of his works, completing the second and third volumes of Das Kapital.
In what year was Edward Teller born?
Edward Teller: Born in Austria-Hungary in 1908, Teller emigrated to the US in the 1930s, one of the many so-called "Martians", a group of Hungarian scientist émigrés.
In what year did J. Robert Oppenheimer die?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year did Kitty Oppenheimer die?
Kitty Oppenheimer: Robert Oppenheimer, the director of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II.
In what year was Fructose discovered?
Fructose, or fruit sugar, is a common monosaccharide, i.e. a simple sugar.
In what year was Gallium discovered?
Gallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ga and atomic number 31.
Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control
Lorazepam: Pfizer. Lorazepam, sold under the brand name Ativan among others, is a benzodiazepine medication.
Which country is AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo from?
AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo: Taiwan. The aircraft made its first flight in 1989.
Who is credited with discovering Plutonium?
Plutonium: Glenn Theodore Seaborg. Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
Who is credited with discovering Fermium?
Fermium: Glenn Theodore Seaborg. Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.
Who is credited with discovering Sodium?
Sodium: Humphry Davy. Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.
Taken as a pill, cream, or injection, this antiviral medication is the go-to treatment for herpes simplex, chickenpox, and shingles — what is it?
Aciclovir is an antiviral medication. It is primarily used for the treatment of herpes simplex virus infections, chickenpox, and shingles.
This amphoteric compound forms a gelatinous precipitate in water and occurs naturally as the mineral gibbsite, one of bauxite's key components — what is it?
Aluminium hydroxide is a white chemical compound that is found as the mineral gibbsite (also known as hydrargillite) and its three much rarer polymorphs: bayerite, doyleite, and nordstrandite.
This scientific discipline bridges biology and sociology, studying human behavior, cultures, societies, and languages across time. What field is it?

Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity that crosses biology and sociology, concerned with human behavior, human biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, in both the present and past, including archaic humans.
First described in 1740, this flowering-plant family rivals only the orchid family in sheer number of species, with over 32,000 recognized today — what family is it?
Asteraceae is a large family of flowering plants that consists of over 32,000 known species in over 1,900 genera within the order Asterales.
Designed to replace the aging Tu-126 'Moss,' this Soviet early-warning aircraft saw only about 42 built before the USSR's breakup ended production in 1992 — what is it?
Beriev A-50 (NATO reporting name: Mainstay) is a Soviet-origin airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft that is based on the Ilyushin Il-76 transport plane.
Once known as the Russian Wolfhound until a 1936 name change, this elegant sighthound breed was historically used to hunt wolves — what breed is it?
Borzoi is a Russian breed of hunting dog of sighthound type.
This highly soluble white crystalline salt is commonly spread on roads for de-icing and dust control, and its hygroscopic nature lets it pull moisture straight from the air — what compound is it?
Calcium chloride is an inorganic compound, a salt with the chemical formula CaCl2.
This usually bacterial infection of the skin's inner layers causes spreading redness, swelling, and pain, most often on the legs or face, sometimes accompanied by fever — what is it?
Cellulitis is usually a bacterial infection involving the inner layers of the skin. It specifically affects the dermis and subcutaneous fat.
Resembling an oversized lemon with a thick, coarse rind, this large fragrant citrus fruit is one of the original ancestors from which all other citrus varieties developed — which fruit?

Citron (Citrus medica) is a large fragrant citrus fruit with a thick, coarse rind. It is one of the original citrus fruits from which all other citrus types developed through natural hybrid speciation or artificial hybridization.
This inorganic compound's blue crystalline pentahydrate form was historically called blue vitriol, while its anhydrous form is white and dissolves in water to form an octahedral complex. What is it?
Copper(II) sulfate is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula CuSO4.
This American biologist, who later ran Caltech and founded the Whitehead Institute, won a Nobel at just 37 for discovering the enzyme reverse transcriptase. Who was he?
David Baltimore (March 7, 1938 - September 6, 2025) was an American biologist, university administrator, and 1975 Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine.

Its name comes from a Greek word meaning 'deed' or 'act,' and Aristotle's Poetics contrasted it with the epic and lyric modes; two masks for comedy and tragedy are its emblem. What mode of fiction is it?
Drama is the specific mode of fiction represented in performance: a play, opera, mime, ballet, etc., performed in a theatre, or on radio or television.

These ductless glands throughout the body secrete their products directly into the bloodstream rather than through a duct — together with the pineal, pituitary, thyroid, and others, what are they called?
Endocrine gland is a network of glands and organs located throughout the body.

Mostly caused by a mutation in the PRNP gene, this neurodegenerative prion disease begins with gradually worsening sleep trouble and progresses to total sleeplessness, speech and coordination problems, and death within months — which disease?
Fatal insomnia is a neurodegenerative prion disease that results in trouble sleeping as its hallmark symptom.
After working in Feynman's group on the Manhattan Project, this physicist later co-detected a famously elusive elementary particle, winning the 1995 Nobel — who was he?
Frederick Reines (March 16, 1918 - August 26, 1998) was an American physicist.

This metabolic pathway builds glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, occurring mainly in the liver in vertebrates, and serves as one of the body's two main tools for maintaining blood sugar — what process is it?
Gluconeogenesis (GNG) is a metabolic pathway that results in the biosynthesis of glucose from certain non-carbohydrate carbon substrates.
This Austrian physician wrote over 300 publications and termed his diagnosis of autism 'autistic psychopathy,' though later allegations tied him to a Nazi-era clinic in Vienna — what was his name?
Hans Asperger (18 February 1906 - 21 October 1980) was an Austrian physician.
This common household insect, likely originating in the Middle East, mates only once in her lifetime but stores the sperm to fertilize repeated batches of about 100 eggs — what insect is it?
Housefly (Musca domestica) is a fly of the suborder Cyclorrhapha.
Once extracted from the leaves of Indigofera plants and now mostly made synthetically, this insoluble blue colorant is famous for dyeing denim and enabling tricks like stone washing. What is it?
Indigo dye is an organic compound with a distinctive blue color.
This American psychiatrist and Communist Party USA member is best remembered today for her romantic relationship with J. Robert Oppenheimer — who was she?
Jean Tatlock (February 21, 1914 - January 4, 1944) was an American psychiatrist.
This Afghan-American author sought asylum in the U.S. as a teenager and later wrote a bestselling debut novel set in his homeland before working as a UNHCR goodwill ambassador — who is he?
Khaled Hosseini (Pashto/; born March 4, 1965) is an Afghan and American novelist, UNHCR goodwill ambassador, and former physician.
Caused by Mycobacterium bacteria, this ancient nerve-damaging disease can dull a person's sense of pain so badly that unnoticed wounds cost them their fingers and toes — what is it?
Leprosy (HD), is a long-term infection by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae or Mycobacterium lepromatosis.
This German physicist gave aerodynamics its rigorous mathematical footing, identifying the boundary layer and lifting-line theory — and a dimensionless number bears his name. Who was he?
Ludwig Prandtl (German; 4 February 1875 - 15 August 1953) was a German fluid dynamicist, physicist and aerospace scientist.
Known by a nickname, this Swedish programmer created Minecraft, the best-selling video game in history, and founded the studio Mojang in 2009 — who is he?
Markus Persson (born 1 June 1979), known by the pseudonym Notch, is a Swedish video game programmer and designer.
What neurological disorder causes moderate-to-severe, often one-sided headaches, frequently accompanied by nausea, light and sound sensitivity, and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura'?
Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes moderate-to-severe headaches. The pain usually affects one side of the head.
With shells that are elongated and wedge-shaped rather than round, these bivalves attach themselves to shorelines using threads nicknamed a "beard" — what are they?
Mussel is the common name used for members of several families of bivalve molluscs, from saltwater and freshwater habitats.
A reddish-brown gas that's a key step in making nitric acid for fertilizer, it also seeps into homes from gas-stove cooking and harms indoor air — which compound, formula NO2?
Nitrogen dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula NO2.
Usually caused by bacteria and sometimes requiring amputation in severe cases, this infectious inflammation of bone can be acute or chronic — which condition?
Osteomyelitis (OM) is the infectious inflammation of bone. It may be acute or chronic and can be classified as hematogenous or non-hematogenous.
Commercially produced from citrus fruits as a white-to-light-brown powder, this plant-cell-wall polysaccharide is the gelling agent that makes jams and jellies set — what is it?
Pectin (Ancient) is a heteropolysaccharide, a structural polymer contained in the cell walls and middle lamellae of terrestrial plants.
These drifting, self-feeding members of the plankton community photosynthesize like land plants, so they crowd the sunlit surface waters of oceans and lakes — what are they?
Phytoplankton are the autotrophic (self-feeding) components of the plankton community and a key part of ocean and freshwater ecosystems.
This American actor and mixed martial artist is best known for playing a heroic ranger across a Power Rangers television franchise. Who is he?
Potassium hydroxide is an inorganic compound with the formula KOH, and is commonly called caustic potash.
One of America's top rocketry and high-speed-flight experts, this engineer helped found engineering cybernetics before being deported to China in 1955. Who was he?

Qian Xuesen (December 11, 1911 - October 31, 2009; also spelled as Tsien Hsue-shen) was a Chinese aerospace engineer and cyberneticist who made significant contributions to the field of aerodynamics and established engineering cybernetics.
As chairman of the now-defunct Purdue Pharma, he oversaw the launch of OxyContin — a tenure dramatized in Hulu's Dopesick and Netflix's Painkiller; who is he?
Richard Sackler (born March 10, 1945) is an American businessman, pharmaceutical entrepreneur and physician who was the chairman and president of Purdue Pharma, a now-defunct pharmaceutical company.

Created by Martin Odersky to address criticisms of Java, this statically typed tool blends object-oriented and functional styles, compiles to JVM bytecode, and can even transpile to JavaScript — which one?
Scala (programming language) is a strongly statically typed high-level general-purpose programming language that supports both object-oriented programming and functional programming.
Element number 14 is a tetravalent non-metal sometimes called a metalloid, prized for the transistors and integrated circuits it makes possible — which one is it?
Silicon is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
The largest order of reptiles, this group is set apart by movable quadrate bones that let snakes gape their jaws around oversized prey — what's the order called?
Squamata (Latin squamatus, 'scaly, having scales') is the largest order of reptiles; most members of which are commonly known as lizards, with the group also including snakes.

This genus of about a dozen woody flowering shrubs in the olive family, native from southeastern Europe to East Asia, is closely related to privet and provides food for several moth larvae — what is it commonly called?
Syringa is a genus of 12 currently recognized species of flowering woody plants in the olive family called lilacs.
This condition causes abnormally low platelet levels in the blood, leading to prolonged or excessive bleeding — what blood disorder is it?
Thrombocytopenia is a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of platelets (also known as thrombocytes) in the blood.
An important food fish found in marine and brackish waters from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, this flatfish's Black Sea relatives are now classified as a separate species — which fish?
Turbot is a relatively large species of flatfish in the family Scophthalmidae.
Leading organic chemistry at DuPont's Experimental Station, this troubled chemist not only invented nylon but also helped lay the groundwork for neoprene. Who was he?
Wallace Carothers (April 27, 1896 - April 29, 1937) was an American chemist, inventor, and the leader of organic chemistry at DuPont, who was credited with the invention of nylon.

Nicknamed the 'Sleeping Dragon' during his years in seclusion, this Chinese strategist was sought out three times by a warlord before becoming chancellor of the Shu Han state and, later, regent to its young second emperor — who is he?

Zhuge Liang (181 AD - September or October 234 AD), courtesy name Kongming, was a Chinese statesman and strategist who lived through the collapse of the Eastern Han dynasty and became the principal architect of the Shu Han state.
This nucleoside, a building block of RNA, gives rise to the energy carriers ATP and ADP and is used as an intravenous drug for certain irregular heartbeats — what is it?
Working at a Soviet computing centre in 1985, this engineer designed one of history's most famous puzzle games — yet saw no royalties from it until founding a company around it in 1996. Who is he?
Caused by the parasite Entamoeba histolytica, this intestinal infection can spread to the liver and trigger abscesses there even without any prior diarrhea — what condition is it?
Amoebiasis: Human disease caused by amoeba protists.

Their larvae — nicknamed "doodlebugs" in North America for the marks they leave — dig sandy pits to trap passing ants, while the dusk-flying adults are often mistaken for dragonflies. What insect is this?
These chitin-armored invertebrates must shed their exoskeletons to grow and circulate haemolymph through an open body cavity — and may number up to ten million species. What are they?
Arthropod: Phylum of invertebrates with jointed exoskeletons.

Flown by the Royal Air Force's Red Arrows display team, this British jet-powered advanced trainer has been license-built in India by Hindustan Aeronautics, with over 1,000 sold to 18 countries — which aircraft?
BAE Systems Hawk: Military training aircraft family.
Originating in the Swiss Alps' canton of Bern, this large farm breed historically pulled carts for alpine herders and traces its ancestry to Roman mastiffs — which breed, recognized in 1912?
Bernese Mountain Dog: Swiss breed of dog. The Bernese Mountain Dog, German: Berner Sennenhund or Dürrbächler, is a large dog breed originating from the canton of Bern, Switzerland and the Swiss Alps.
Originally launched as the McDonnell Douglas MD-95, this narrow-body airliner seats up to 134 passengers with twin engines mounted at the tail — which jet?

He won a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics for an effect he discovered as a Cambridge PhD student in 1962 — then, in the 1970s, took up Transcendental Meditation and pursued ideas beyond mainstream science. Who is he?
Its dihydrate form is the mineral gypsum and its dehydrated cousin is bassanite; sparingly soluble, it causes permanent hardness in water — which inorganic salt is this?
Calcium sulfate: Chemical derived from gypsum used in food and industry.
A nerve compression syndrome caused when the median nerve in the wrist becomes compressed, causing numbness and tingling in the thumb and fingers. What is this condition?
Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve in the wrist. It can also be measured with electrodiagnostic tests.
Also known as silver beet or perpetual spinach, this leafy green shares its species with beetroot — which vegetable?
Chard: Green leafy vegetable. Chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, Cicla Group and Flavescens Group) is a green leafy vegetable.
Sold under the brand name Celexa, this SSRI antidepressant treats major depressive disorder, OCD, panic disorder, and social anxiety — what is it?
Citalopram: SSRI antidepressant. Citalopram, sold under the brand name Celexa among others, is an antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class.
This bird family contains both doves and pigeons — including the feral rock dove common in cities — spanning 52 genera and 353 species worldwide. What's the family called?
Columbidae: Family of birds. The bird most commonly referred to as "pigeon" is the domestic pigeon, descendant of the wild rock dove, which is a common inhabitant of cities as the feral pigeon.
First appearing in English in 1656 and later formalized in Latin by philosopher Christian Wolff, this field of study addresses the nature and origin of the universe — what field is it?
Cosmology: Study of the universe. Cosmology (from Ancient Greek κόσμος (cosmos) 'the universe, the world' and -λογία (logia) 'study of') is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
This biological process lets a cell make an exact copy of its genetic material by using each strand of the double helix as a template for a new one — what is it called?
DNA replication: Biological process. DNA replication ensures that each of the newly divided daughter cells receives its own copy of each DNA molecule.
A volatile, colorless liquid with a sweet, chloroform-like smell, this organochlorine (formula CH2Cl2) is slightly polar, won't mix with water, and is prized as a widely-used solvent. What is it?
Marketed as Cymbalta, this serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor treats depression, anxiety, and fibromyalgia pain — what is it?
Co-founding Mattel with his wife Ruth, this inventor helped bring Barbie, Hot Wheels, and Chatty Cathy to toy shelves — who is he?
Elliot Handler: American inventor and business magnate (1916–2011)
Made by yeast fermenting sugars and once used as a general anesthetic, this colorless flammable liquid is the world's second most consumed drug, behind only caffeine — what is it?
This front-of-the-head body part houses most sense organs — eyes, nose, and mouth — and its damage or scarring can profoundly affect a person's sense of identity. What is it?
Face: Front of a head. The face is the front of the head in humans and many other animals that features most of the sense organs including the eyes, nose and mouth.
Belonging to a bird family that's the only survivor of its order, this wading bird comes in four American species plus two more across Africa and Eurasia — what is it?
Flamingo: Family of birds. There are four flamingo species distributed throughout the Americas (including the Caribbean), and two species native to Afro-Eurasia.
Sold under the brand name Lasix, this loop diuretic treats edema from heart failure and kidney disease and can also cause tinnitus and light sensitivity?

Furosemide: Loop diuretic medication. Furosemide, sold under the brand name Lasix among others, is a loop diuretic medication used to treat edema due to heart failure, liver scarring, or kidney disease.

The largest species of its kind in the world, this circumglobal sea creature was reclassified in 2017 after DNA testing showed it was more closely related to a different genus than to its smaller reef-dwelling cousin — what is it?
Giant oceanic manta ray: Species of cartilaginous fish.
Known as the black shag in New Zealand, this widespread seabird breeds across much of the Old World, Australasia, and the Atlantic coast of North America — which bird?

Recognizable by V-shaped nostrils and a layer of blubber that keeps it warm in Arctic and temperate coastal waters, this pinniped is the most widely distributed of its kind and can weigh up to 370 pounds — which species?
Harbor seal: Species of pinniped. Blubber under the seal's skin helps to maintain body temperature.
In this condition, part of the stomach slips upward through the diaphragm into the chest, often triggering acid reflux, heartburn, or trouble swallowing — what is it?
Hiatal hernia: Entrance of abdominal organs into the middle chest through the diaphragm.
Also called prussic acid, this toxic, flammable liquid with the formula HCN boils just above room temperature and serves as an industrial precursor to plastics and mining chemicals — what is it?

Also known as the spectacled or binocellate snake, this reptile from South Asia is one of the 'Big Four' species responsible for most snakebites in the region and is revered in Hindu mythology — which snake?
Indian cobra: Species of snake. The species is native to the Indian subcontinent, and is a member of the "Big Four" species that are responsible for the most snakebite cases in Sri Lanka and India.
This English inventor and industrial designer created the bagless vacuum cleaner using cyclonic separation, and by 2023 was the UK's fifth-richest person — who is he?
James Dyson: British inventor and businessman (born 1947)
Back in 1859, this Irish physicist proved the link between atmospheric CO2 and what we now call the greenhouse effect — who was he?
This term for certain birds of prey comes from an Old English word imitating a buzzard's call, and by 1768 had become fixed on one particular reddish, forked-tailed species — what's this common name?
Kite (bird): Index of animals with the same common name.
This genus of bacteria mainly infects amoebae but can cause a pneumonia-like illness in humans when it spreads via poorly maintained cooling towers — what genus is it?
Legionella: Pathogenic genus of Gram-negative bacteria.
Only about 35 atoms of this synthetic element (number 116) had ever been made as of 2020 — and it's named for the California national laboratory that helped discover it. Which element?
Livermorium: Chemical element with atomic number 116 (Lv)

Originally built at a Boston hospital to manage patient records, this programming language pairs directly with an integrated key-value database and now underpins Epic's electronic health records — which language?
MUMPS: Programming language. It was originally developed at Massachusetts General Hospital for managing patient medical records and hospital laboratory information systems.
Known by the pseudonym 'Notch,' this Swedish programmer created the best-selling video game of all time and became a billionaire when Microsoft bought his studio for $2.5 billion in 2014 — who is he?
Markus Persson: Swedish video game programmer (born 1979)
This rose-family shrub, commonly known as the medlar, produces fruit that's traditionally eaten only after it has softened past ripeness — what's its scientific name?
Mespilus germanica: Fruit tree, the medlar. Mespilus germanica, known as the medlar or common medlar, is a large shrub or small tree in the rose family Rosaceae.

The only woman among Einstein's classmates at Zurich Polytechnic, this Serbian mathematician was his first wife and is still debated as a possible collaborator on his 1905 miracle-year papers. Who was she?
Mileva Marić: Wife of Albert Einstein (1875–1948)
With a pointed snout, round ears, and a scaly tail as long as its body, this small rodent species is usually distinguished from its larger cousin the rat mainly by size — which animal?
Mouse: Small long-tailed rodent. A mouse (pl. mice) is a small rodent, characteristically known to have a pointed snout, small rounded ears, a body-length scaly tail, and a high breeding rate.
Descended from Southern Italy's traditional guard dogs and closely related to the Cane Corso, this large wrinkly Italian breed was recognized in 1949 — which dog breed?
Neapolitan Mastiff: Italian breed of dog. The Neapolitan Mastiff or Mastino Napoletano is an Italian breed of large dog of mastiff type.

As the United States' first swept-wing fighter jet, this Korean War-era aircraft dueled Soviet MiG-15s in some of history's earliest jet-to-jet battles — which plane, produced in more than 7,800 units?
North American F-86 Sabre: Family of US fighter aircraft.

The world's most widespread and commercially important cactus species, this domesticated crop is grown both as a fruit and for its edible vegetable pads, likely originating in central Mexico — which species?
Opuntia ficus-indica: Species of cactus. It is grown primarily as a fruit crop, and also for the vegetable nopales and other uses.
One researcher catalogued as many as 549 varieties of this psychological category, defined by intense arousal toward things that aren't sexual by nature — what is the term?
In placental mammals, this is the region of the body between the anus and the genitals, running from the pubic bone to the tailbone, and is often considered an erogenous zone — what is it called?
Perineum: Region of the body between the genitals and anus. The perineum (pl.: perineums or perinea) in placental mammals is the space between the anus and the genitals.
Named after the Latin word for the magpie, a bird known for its opportunistic feeding habits, this eating disorder involves craving non-food objects — what is it?
Pica (disorder): Compulsive eating of non-food items.
Named from the Latin word for 'bridge' after Italian anatomist Costanzo Varolio, this brainstem structure sits above the medulla and below the midbrain — what is it?
Pons: Part of the brainstem in humans and other bipeds.
Named after a Russian explorer and reintroduced to Mongolia's steppes after going extinct in the wild, this rare equine has 33 chromosome pairs instead of the usual 32 — what species is it?
Colorless and odorless, this radioactive noble gas with atomic number 86 is a decay product of radium and eventually settles into stable isotopes of lead?
Radon: Chemical element with atomic number 86 (Rn)
Curving around the chest, these bones protect the lungs and heart and, in snakes, support and protect the whole body — what are they called?
Rib: Long bone in vertebrates that protects vital respiratory and cardiovascular organs.
